title: Episode 4: The Learning Room
description: Your shared practice environment: challenges, PR workflow, bot feedback, peer review.
concepts: What the Learning Room repository is and its purpose
The fork-edit-PR workflow for submitting solutions
How the automated bot provides feedback on your pull request
Peer review: reading and commenting on classmate work
Why low-stakes practice builds real confidence
How to find your challenge and know when you are done
transcriptText:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we’re getting oriented inside your personal practice space on GitHub. Think of this as your workshop sandbox, but a very real one. It has issues, branches, pull requests, automation, and review workflows, just like a live project.

[JAMIE]
So this is not just a demo repo somebody is showing on screen. It’s my own working repository.

[ALEX]
Exactly. When you accept the GitHub Classroom assignment, GitHub creates a private copy of the workshop template just for you. The template lives in Community-Access slash learning-room-template, but you do not work in that template directly. GitHub Classroom copies it into the workshop organization and names it something like learning-room-your-username.

[JAMIE]
And that copy is mine to experiment in.

[ALEX]
Yes. You get write access, your own branches, your own pull requests, and your own automated bot feedback. Other students are working through the same challenge sequence, but they are doing it in their own private copies. You generally won’t see their work in your repo, and they won’t see yours, unless facilitators intentionally pair people for review.

[JAMIE]
That privacy matters. Especially if someone is learning all of this for the first time.

[ALEX]
It does. And the workshop setup is already managed for you. You do not need to create an organization, change permissions, or wire up GitHub Actions. Facilitators handle the classroom organization, the template, the assignment, and the automation permissions.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Why give every student a separate repository instead of putting everyone into one shared practice repo?

[ALEX]
Three big reasons. Safety, authenticity, and pace. Safety means you can try things, make mistakes, and recover without affecting anyone else. Authenticity means the workflow is real: issues, branches, pull requests, checks, reviews, merging. And pace means you can move as quickly or as slowly as you need through the Day 1 challenges without blocking another learner or waiting on them.

[JAMIE]
So this is rehearsal for open source work, but with guardrails.

[ALEX]
That’s a great way to say it. On Day 2, and in some bonus work, you’ll contribute in a more shared setting. The Learning Room is where you build the muscle memory first: issue, branch, pull request, review, merge.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let’s walk through getting into it, because that first entry point can feel intimidating.

[ALEX]
Absolutely. Before you start, you need two things. First, a GitHub account, already signed into your browser. Second, the Day 1 GitHub Classroom assignment link from the facilitator. It usually looks like classroom dot github dot com slash a slash some random ID.

[JAMIE]
And if I don’t have that link, I should ask in chat or message a facilitator.

[ALEX]
Right. Once you open the assignment link in the same browser where you’re signed into GitHub, the page is hosted on classroom dot github dot com. Your screen reader should announce a heading with the assignment name, something like the workshop name and Day 1.

[JAMIE]
And sometimes GitHub Classroom asks for authorization first, right?

[ALEX]
Yes. If you’re prompted to authorize GitHub Classroom to access your GitHub account, activate the authorize button. That’s usually a one-time step.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Then there’s sometimes a roster page.

[ALEX]
Correct. GitHub Classroom may ask you to identify yourself from a roster so facilitators can match your GitHub username to the registration list. If that page appears, move through the list with arrow keys, or use Find in Page, Control F on Windows or Command F on Mac, to search for your name. Activate the link or button next to it.

[JAMIE]
And if my name isn’t there?

[ALEX]
Use the Skip to the next step link, if it’s available, and tell the facilitator in chat. They can reconcile the roster later. The important thing is that your repository still gets created.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Next comes the main acceptance step. Activate the button that says Accept this assignment, or Accept the assignment.

[JAMIE]
What happens behind the scenes there?

[ALEX]
GitHub Classroom starts copying the learning room template into the workshop organization and granting you access to your private copy. You’ll usually land on a status page that says something like, you are ready to go, with a refresh option. This process often takes ten to thirty seconds.

[JAMIE]
And I should keep refreshing until the repository link appears.

[ALEX]
Yes. Every fifteen seconds or so, activate Refresh or reload the page with F5. The finished link will look like github dot com slash workshop-org slash learning-room-your-username.

[JAMIE]
There was also an important screen reader tip in the reading.

[ALEX]
Yes. The status page does not reliably auto-announce when the repository is ready. So if you use a screen reader, switch to browse mode and press K to move by links until you hear your repository link, or just keep refreshing until it appears.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Once I open the repo, what should I verify?

[ALEX]
Three things. First, the repository heading should match learning-room-your-username. Second, the About area or description should make it clear this is your private workshop copy. Third, you should see template content already there, such as folders like docs and dot github, plus files like README dot md.

[JAMIE]
And bookmark it.

[ALEX]
Definitely bookmark it. You’ll return to this repository throughout Day 1.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now the first real action inside the repo: finding the first challenge issue.

[ALEX]
Right. Once your Learning Room is ready, Challenge 1 should appear as a GitHub issue. Facilitators use the Student Progression Bot to prepare that sequence, and later challenges unlock one at a time as you complete earlier ones.

[JAMIE]
So from the repository page, I go to Issues.

[ALEX]
Yes. You can use the Issues tab, or GitHub’s keyboard shortcut G then I. Look for an open issue with a title like Challenge 1: Find Your Way Around. The author may be aria-bot or github-actions bot. Open it and read the issue body carefully. It tells you what to do, where to find the evidence, and how to submit completion.

[JAMIE]
What if Challenge 1 isn’t there yet?

[ALEX]
If it’s still missing after about two minutes, refresh the Issues tab once. If it still doesn’t appear, open the Actions tab and check whether the Student Progression Bot workflow ran successfully. If it failed, or never ran, post your repo link in workshop chat. A facilitator can trigger student-progression dot yml or create Challenge 1 from the issue template.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
And then there’s Gandalf.

[ALEX]
Yes, the PR validation bot. To confirm Gandalf can talk to you, open the Actions tab and look for a workflow named pr-validation-bot or Gandalf PR Validation. You don’t need to run anything yet. You’re just checking that the workflow exists in your repository before you start making pull requests.

[JAMIE]
So by that point, Block 0 is really complete: repo created, first issue present or troubleshootable, automation visible.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
This part of the workshop is orientation, not a challenge chapter. There are no challenge completions to submit here and no automation checks to pass yet. The purpose is to help you understand the system before the issue-based work begins.

[JAMIE]
So what should a learner be able to do before moving on?

[ALEX]
Three readiness checks. One, find docs slash CHALLENGES dot md in the repository. Two, explain the basic workflow: issue to branch to pull request to review to merge. Three, identify where Gandalf bot feedback appears on a pull request, which is the Conversation tab.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
The chapter also described two learning tracks happening at the same time. That seems important, because people may confuse them.

[ALEX]
Very important. Throughout Day 1, you may be working in two related but different tracks under your own GitHub account. Track 1 is GitHub Skills modules. These are optional, self-paced exercises from GitHub, such as Introduction to GitHub, Communicate Using Markdown, and Review Pull Requests.

[JAMIE]
That’s the path where GitHub’s learning bot, Mona, guides you step by step.

[ALEX]
Exactly. The scope there is your personal account, and the purpose is focused practice on individual skills like creating a branch, writing Markdown, or reviewing a PR.

[JAMIE]
And Track 2 is the required workshop track inside the Learning Room.

[ALEX]
Yes. That’s where your Day 1 challenge sequence lives. The reading described it as blocks across the day, with challenges that include getting oriented, filing an issue, creating a branch, committing, opening a pull request, handling merge conflict practice, and then later community and merge-focused work, plus community tools like labels, milestones, and notifications.

[JAMIE]
So the tracks reinforce each other, but they are not the same thing.

[ALEX]
Precisely. One is optional self-paced skills practice. The other is the required workshop experience. They use the same GitHub account, but different repositories, different bots, and different goals.

[JAMIE]
That sounds like a good learning card summary: two tracks, one account.

[ALEX]
Exactly that. If you ever feel confused, ask yourself: am I in a GitHub Skills training repo, or am I in my private Learning Room repo for the workshop?

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let’s talk about the repository layout. Even if we don’t list every file on air, learners need a mental map.

[ALEX]
Right. Your Learning Room has a deliberate folder structure. You’ll commonly encounter the docs folder, which holds most of the practice content and challenge materials. You’ll also see dot github, which contains automation-related files such as workflows and issue or pull request templates. And you’ll see top-level files like README dot md.

[JAMIE]
So when someone is browsing with a screen reader or keyboard, it helps to know what kinds of places they’re looking for.

[ALEX]
Exactly. The docs folder is where much of your reading and editing work happens. The dot github folder tends to support the automation and workflow side of the experience.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now let’s talk branches, because this is where many beginners freeze. What is the practice branch for?

[ALEX]
Your practice branch is the branch you create to do challenge work without editing the default branch directly. The reason for a separate branch is simple but foundational: it gives you an isolated workspace for changes, makes pull requests possible, preserves a clean main branch, and mirrors real collaboration patterns used in open source projects.

[JAMIE]
So even though this is my own repo, I still use a branch because I’m practicing the real workflow.

[ALEX]
Exactly. The branch is not about distrust. It’s about process. Open the issue, create or switch to your practice branch, make the changes there, commit them, and then open a pull request back into the default branch.

[JAMIE]
And if I leave and come back later?

[ALEX]
You need to make sure you’re on the correct branch before editing. That’s part of the tool-card idea here: know how to switch to your practice branch in whichever interface you’re using, whether on the GitHub website or in VS Code. Branch awareness prevents a lot of confusion.

[JAMIE]
So the branch learning card is really: use a separate branch on purpose, and return to it consciously.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
The chapter also pointed to specific practice files. Let’s walk through what learners will actually work on.

[ALEX]
One important file is docs slash welcome dot md. That file introduces open source contribution ideas. It includes at least three targeted to-do areas.

[JAMIE]
The first is a section about who can contribute.

[ALEX]
Yes. That reinforces a crucial idea: open source contribution is not limited to expert programmers. People contribute documentation, testing, bug reports, accessibility feedback, design suggestions, issue triage, community support, and many other forms of labor.

[JAMIE]
That’s especially important in an accessibility-centered workshop, because contribution includes making things more usable and more inclusive.

[ALEX]
Exactly. The second to-do area is about finding something to work on. That usually means learning how contributors identify tasks through issues, labels, documentation gaps, or starter-friendly opportunities.

[JAMIE]
So not just waiting to be told what to do, but learning how work is discovered.

[ALEX]
Right. And the third to-do area is about what happens after your contribution is merged. That helps normalize that merging is not the end of the story. There may be follow-up discussion, more contributions, maintenance, and continued community participation.

[JAMIE]
That’s a healthy expectation to set early.

[ALEX]
It is.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Another practice file is docs slash keyboard-shortcuts dot md, a screen reader shortcut reference.

[JAMIE]
That sounds especially relevant to this audience.

[ALEX]
Very much so. It gives learners a place to practice and document useful commands they’ll rely on when navigating GitHub, reading pages efficiently, moving among controls, and working confidently with keyboard and screen reader tools.

[JAMIE]
And there’s docs slash setup-guide dot md.

[ALEX]
Yes. That file is about getting ready to contribute. It supports the practical setup mindset: before contribution comes preparation. That can include understanding tools, account readiness, navigation habits, and the basic workflow expectations that help you succeed once challenges start.

[JAMIE]
And then docs slash CHALLENGES dot md is the menu.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Think of that file as your challenge roadmap. It helps you see what kinds of tasks exist in the Learning Room, even though progression may unlock step by step through issues.

[JAMIE]
And there are bonus challenges too.

[ALEX]
Yes. Bonus challenges let learners go further once required work is complete or when they want extra practice. They’re useful for stretching skills without making the core pathway overwhelming.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now for one of the most important pieces conceptually: how pull request sharing works in this learning environment.

[ALEX]
Yes. The chapter laid this out as a sequence. First, the student opens a pull request.

[JAMIE]
So imagine Student A is working on Challenge 3, maybe completing part of the welcome guide.

[ALEX]
Right. They make changes on their branch, then open a PR into the repository’s main branch. That PR becomes the central place where the work is discussed, checked, and eventually merged.

[JAMIE]
Then automation validates it.

[ALEX]
Yes. Step 2 is the automation bot. A workflow such as dot github slash workflows slash learning-room-pr-bot dot yml, along with the validation system called Gandalf, checks the PR and posts educational feedback. This usually verifies structure or expected evidence, and helps the learner understand what is correct or what still needs attention.

[JAMIE]
So the bot isn’t just policing. It’s teaching.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[JAMIE]
Then comes peer review, but it’s facilitator-arranged.

[ALEX]
Yes. That is an important nuance. Step 3 is not a free-for-all where everyone sees everyone’s work by default. Review access is intentionally arranged. Visibility depends on how the workshop is configured. A facilitator may pair students so one learner can review another learner’s PR.

[JAMIE]
Then Step 4 is the reviewer reading and commenting.

[ALEX]
Right. If you are assigned as a peer reviewer, you read the PR carefully, inspect the changed files, and leave comments or a formal review. Again, visibility is controlled. You review what you have been given access to review, not the entire classroom’s work.

[JAMIE]
Then the author responds and updates.

[ALEX]
Yes. Step 5 is where the PR author reads the feedback, replies if needed, updates their branch, and pushes new commits. The PR updates in place. This is one of the best parts of learning GitHub, because it shows that feedback is part of the workflow, not a sign of failure.

[JAMIE]
And Step 6 is merge and celebration.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Once the review is approved, or in some cases when you decide to self-merge according to workshop rules, the PR is merged. Then the progression bot can post the next challenge. That merge event is not just an ending. It also triggers progress tracking and unlocks what comes next.

[JAMIE]
So the learning card summary would be: open PR, bot checks, peer review if assigned, revise, merge, next challenge unlocks.

[ALEX]
Beautifully said.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let’s make the visibility model extra clear. What do you see, and what do your peers see?

[ALEX]
In general, you primarily see your own private Learning Room repository: your issues, your branches, your pull requests, your bot feedback. Other students are in parallel private repos. They do not automatically browse your work, and you do not automatically browse theirs. If the workshop sets up intentional peer review, then specific access is granted for that purpose.

[JAMIE]
That means learners should not assume either extreme. Not fully public, not magical isolation from all collaboration.

[ALEX]
Exactly. It is private by default, with structured collaboration where appropriate.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
The automation system itself had three types of feedback, and that timing matters.

[ALEX]
Yes. Type 1 is automated bot feedback, often around thirty seconds. That is your near-immediate signal after opening or updating a PR. Type 2 is peer reviewer feedback, which may take fifteen to sixty minutes depending on workshop pacing and facilitator pairing. Type 3 is progress tracking on merge, where the system recognizes that a challenge was completed and may unlock or post the next one.

[JAMIE]
That timing helps learners manage anxiety. If nothing happens in ten seconds, it doesn’t mean the whole system is broken.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Know which feedback channel you’re waiting for.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
The reading also mentioned optional study groups.

[ALEX]
Yes. Study groups are optional. They can help learners compare approaches, talk through concepts, or encourage one another. But they do not replace your own repository workflow. Even if you work alongside a partner or small group, each learner still needs to complete their own work in their own Learning Room unless facilitators say otherwise.

[JAMIE]
So collaboration is allowed, but ownership of the actual repo work stays individual.

[ALEX]
Correct. The example idea there is learning together while still submitting your own contribution path.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Can we sharpen the difference between a GitHub Skills module and the Learning Room one more time?

[ALEX]
Certainly. In a GitHub Skills module, the environment is a training repo, the guide is usually Mona, and the lesson is narrowly structured around one skill. In the Learning Room, the environment is your private workshop repository, the guidance comes from workshop issues, bots, documentation, and facilitators, and the goal is integrated practice across a realistic contribution workflow.

[JAMIE]
So a Skills module might teach one isolated move, while the Learning Room teaches how the moves connect.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now let’s talk about reviewing a peer’s pull request, because learners often know how to ask for feedback before they know how to give it.

[ALEX]
A few practical tips. First, finding PRs to review. In this workshop, that often means using the link or access a facilitator provides, rather than browsing a public queue. Once you have the PR, open it and orient yourself to the Conversation tab, the Files changed tab, and any bot feedback already posted.

[JAMIE]
Then reading the PR you’re assigned to.

[ALEX]
Yes. Start with the PR description. Understand what challenge the author was trying to complete. Then inspect the changed files with curiosity and care. Ask: does the change meet the stated goal, and is it clear, respectful, and complete?

[JAMIE]
What makes a good review comment?

[ALEX]
A good review is specific, actionable, and kind. Point to a concrete line or idea. Say what works well when something is strong. If something needs revision, explain why and suggest a next step. Avoid vague comments like “fix this.”

[JAMIE]
And if I’m the author responding to feedback?

[ALEX]
Read generously. Ask clarifying questions if needed. Make updates on your branch, push them, and reply in the PR so the reviewer knows what changed. You do not need to treat feedback as personal criticism. It is part of collaborative improvement.

[JAMIE]
That sounds like the PR sharing learning card in plain language: locate the PR, read with context, leave kind specific comments, and respond constructively.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let’s run through the FAQ-style concerns, because these are the questions people often hesitate to ask aloud.

[ALEX]
Great idea.

[JAMIE]
Can I see other students’ PRs?

[ALEX]
Usually not by default. Access is generally limited to your own repository unless facilitators arrange visibility for peer review or another workshop purpose.

[JAMIE]
What if I don’t agree with my assigned reviewer?

[ALEX]
Treat that as a conversation, not a conflict. Ask clarifying questions, explain your reasoning respectfully, and involve a facilitator if needed. Review comments are part of learning, and not every disagreement is a problem.

[JAMIE]
Will my PR get lost when everyone is working at once?

[ALEX]
Not if the workflow is functioning normally. Your PR lives in your repository, with bot checks and workshop processes around it. If something seems stalled unusually long, that’s when you check the relevant tabs and ask for help.

[JAMIE]
Can I comment on someone else’s PR?

[ALEX]
Only when you have access and when that interaction fits workshop expectations. Don’t assume broad visibility. Follow facilitator guidance.

[JAMIE]
What if my reviewer doesn’t respond?

[ALEX]
Wait a reasonable amount of time, remembering that peer review may take fifteen to sixty minutes or more depending on the session. Then notify a facilitator. Don’t stay stuck silently.

[JAMIE]
Can I work with a friend?

[ALEX]
You can often study with a friend or discuss ideas, especially in optional study groups, but each person should still complete their own repository work unless the facilitators explicitly set up something collaborative.

[JAMIE]
How long does review take?

[ALEX]
Bot feedback may appear in about thirty seconds. Human review often takes longer, commonly fifteen to sixty minutes in the workshop model described.

[JAMIE]
What if bot feedback is wrong?

[ALEX]
That can happen. Automation is helpful, not infallible. Re-read the issue and PR requirements, compare them to your work, and ask a facilitator if the bot seems incorrect. Treat the bot as a guide, not the final authority.

[JAMIE]
Do I need to complete every challenge?

[ALEX]
Follow the workshop expectations for required challenges, and use bonus challenges as extra practice where appropriate. The exact completion target can depend on pacing, but the core challenge sequence is there for a reason.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
If someone gets stuck anywhere in this system, what’s the advice?

[ALEX]
First, pause and identify where you are in the workflow. Are you trying to find the repo, locate an issue, switch branches, open a PR, interpret bot feedback, or wait for review? Second, check the relevant tab: Issues, Pull Requests, Actions, or the Conversation tab in the PR. Third, use the workshop chat or contact a facilitator with a specific question and, if possible, the link to the repo or PR.

[JAMIE]
So not just “it’s broken,” but “I’m in my Learning Room, Challenge 1 is missing,” or “my PR bot feedback says something I don’t understand.”

[ALEX]
Exactly. Specific context gets you help faster.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
I also want to underline something emotional here. Opening issues and pull requests in a learning repo can still feel vulnerable.

[ALEX]
It can. But that’s why this environment exists. You are contributing in a structured, supportive space designed for learning. Every branch you create, every issue you open, every PR you revise, every comment you leave thoughtfully, that is real contribution practice.

[JAMIE]
So even though it’s a classroom setup, it is still authentic contribution behavior.

[ALEX]
Yes. You are learning the habits that make open source participation possible: clarity, iteration, review, and collaboration. That deserves celebration.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Before we wrap, two administrative reminders from the reading. There is a podcast version of this chapter you can use before or after reading as reinforcement, and the appendices like the glossary and Markdown reference remain useful companions as you work. The chapter also pointed to authoritative GitHub documentation, especially around README files, editing files, GitHub flow, Git, and pull requests. Those are excellent references whenever you want the official version of how a feature works.

[JAMIE]
So the takeaway is: get into your private Learning Room, confirm the first issue and the bots are there, understand the two-track model, use branches on purpose, work through the practice files, and expect a real pull request workflow with automation and possibly peer review.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Once that mental model clicks, the rest of Day 1 becomes much easier to navigate.

[JAMIE]
And if you’re listening as a blind or low-vision learner, remember that the workflow is absolutely navigable with keyboard and screen reader strategies. Use the page structure, GitHub shortcuts where they help, browse mode commands like moving by links, and don’t hesitate to bookmark the key places you return to often.

[ALEX]
Beautifully said. You have your own space. You have a process. And you are ready to start contributing.

# The Learning Room: Your Personal Practice Repository
>
> **Listen to Episode 4:** [The Learning Room](../admin/PODCASTS.md) - a conversational audio overview of this chapter. Listen before reading to preview the concepts, or after to reinforce what you learned.

> **Related appendices:** [Appendix A: Glossary](appendix-a-glossary.md) | [Appendix C: Markdown Reference](appendix-c-markdown-reference.md)
> **Authoritative sources:** [GitHub Docs: About README files](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/managing-your-repositorys-settings-and-features/customizing-your-repository/about-readmes) | [GitHub Docs: Editing files](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/working-with-files/managing-files/editing-files)

## What Is the Learning Room?

The **Learning Room** is your **own private GitHub repository** for the workshop. When you accept the GitHub Classroom assignment in Block 0, GitHub copies the [`Community-Access/learning-room-template`](https://github.com/Community-Access/learning-room-template) repository into the workshop classroom organization as `<workshop-org>/learning-room-<your-username>`. That copy is yours to use for the workshop - you have write access, your own branches, your own pull requests, and your own automated feedback from Gandalf the PR validation bot.

You do **not** work directly in `Community-Access/learning-room-template`. Think of the template as the clean master copy facilitators maintain. Your work happens in the private Learning Room repository created for you by GitHub Classroom.

Throughout this chapter and the rest of Day 1, "your Learning Room repository" or "your Learning Room repo" refers to this private copy. Every student gets one, and every copy starts from the same template files. You will not see other students' work in your repo, and they will not see yours - but everyone is doing the same challenges in parallel. Peer-simulation issues and pull requests inside your repo provide realistic collaboration practice, and facilitators may also pair students for real peer review when access is intentionally provided.

You do **not** need to create a GitHub organization or change repository permission settings. The workshop organization, template repository, Classroom assignment, and GitHub Actions permissions are managed by the facilitators.

## Why a Per-Student Repo?

GitHub Classroom gives each participant their own repository for three reasons:

- **Safety** -- you can experiment, break things, and recover without affecting anyone else
- **Authenticity** -- you practice real repository work: issues, branches, pull requests, checks, reviews, and merging
- **Pace** -- you progress through the 9 Day 1 challenges as fast or as slow as you need; nobody is waiting on you and you are not blocking anybody else

Real open source projects are shared spaces, and you will absolutely contribute to one on Day 2 (`accessibility-agents`) and through the Bonus C challenge. The Learning Room exists so you can build the muscle memory for issue, branch, PR, review, merge in a space where every mistake is a learning opportunity, not a public problem.

## Step-by-Step: Accept Your Classroom Assignment and Open Your Repo

This is the very first hands-on step of Day 1. By the end of this walkthrough you will have your own Learning Room repository on GitHub and your first challenge issue waiting for you. The whole flow takes about five minutes.

> **What you need before you start:**
>
> - A GitHub account you are signed into in your browser ([Pre-Workshop Setup, Step 1](00-pre-workshop-setup.md#step-1---create-your-github-account))
> - The **Day 1 Classroom assignment link** -- the facilitator pastes this link in the workshop chat at the start of Block 0. It looks like `https://classroom.github.com/a/<random-id>`. If you do not have it, ask in chat or DM the facilitator.

### 1. Open the assignment link

1. In the same browser where you are signed into GitHub, open the Day 1 assignment link the facilitator shared.
2. The page that loads is hosted on `classroom.github.com`. Your screen reader announces a heading with the assignment name (for example, "Git Going with GitHub -- Day 1").
3. If the page asks you to authorize **GitHub Classroom** to access your GitHub account, activate **Authorize GitHub Classroom**. This is a one-time step.

### 2. Identify yourself (if asked)

GitHub Classroom may ask you to pick your name from a roster so the facilitators can match your GitHub username to the registration list.

1. If a roster page appears, navigate the list with arrow keys or use Find-in-Page (`Ctrl+F` / `Cmd+F`) to search for your name.
2. Activate the link or button next to your name.
3. If you do not see your name on the roster, activate the **Skip to the next step** link and tell the facilitator in chat. They will reconcile the roster after your repo is created.

## Your Practice Branch

In your own Learning Room repository, **you decide what branches to create**. The Day 1 challenge sequence asks you to work on a single feature branch named after yourself:

> **Branch naming convention for Day 1:** `learn/<your-github-username>` (all lowercase)

**Examples:**
- If your GitHub username is `payown`, your branch is `learn/payown`
- If your username is `BudgieMom`, your branch is `learn/budgiemom`
- If your username is `Weijun-Zhang-1996`, your branch is `learn/weijun-zhang-1996`

### Why you create a separate branch

- **Protected main branch** - The `main` branch in your Learning Room is protected; changes have to land via pull request even though you own the repo. This mirrors how mature open source projects work.
- **Your workspace** - Your `learn/<username>` branch is where you commit and push changes before opening a PR
- **Clean history** - Keeping experiments off `main` until they are reviewed (by you, by Gandalf, or by a peer) keeps your project history easy to read
- **Realistic workflow** - Contributors to real open source projects always create feature branches before opening a PR. You are practicing exactly that pattern.

### How to use your branch

The Day 1 challenges (4 onward) walk you through creating and using your branch on GitHub.com. Once you start working locally in Chapter 14, the same branch is what you check out:

```bash
git checkout learn/<your-github-username>
```

1. Create the branch on GitHub.com (Challenge 4) or locally with `git checkout -b learn/<username>` from `main`
2. Make your changes and commit them to the branch
3. Push the branch to GitHub if you created it locally
4. Open a pull request from `learn/<username>` -> `main` (Challenge 6)

> **Which branch do I use and when?**
>
> | Chapter | Branch needed? | What to use |
> |---------|---------------|-------------|
> | Chapter 5 (Issues) | No | Work happens in issue threads directly. No branch or file editing required. |
> | Chapter 6 (PRs, web editor) | Yes | Create `learn/<username>` from `main` (Challenge 4) and edit on it. |
> | Chapter 6 (PRs, local clone) | Yes, create manually | `git checkout -b learn/<username>` from `main`. |
> | Chapter 14+ (Local Git) | Yes | Reuse `learn/<username>`, or create additional `fix/<short-description>` branches from `main` for new work. |
>
> **Summary:** Chapter 5 needs no branch. Chapters 6-7 use the same `learn/<username>` branch. Day 2 reuses that branch and adds short-lived `fix/` branches when you tackle additional issues.

## How PR Sharing Works

### Step 1: Student Opens a PR

#### Student A (working on Challenge 3: Complete Welcome Guide)

1. Finds their assigned issue (Issues tab → filter `Assignee:@me`)
2. Opens `docs/welcome.md` and edits the three `[TODO]` sections
3. Commits to a new branch: `fix/studentA-issue12`
4. Opens a pull request with description:

   ```markdown
   ## What Changed
   Completed the three [TODO] sections in docs/welcome.md:
   - Added contributor backgrounds paragraph
   - Added guidance on evaluating issues
   - Added note about GitHub profile impact

   Closes #12
   ```

5. **Submits the PR**

**Visibility:** The PR immediately appears in the repo's Pull Requests tab. All students can see it.

### Step 2: Automation Bot Validates

#### Bot (`.github/workflows/learning-room-pr-bot.yml`)

- Runs within 30 seconds
- Checks:
  - Issue reference (does PR link to issue with `Closes #12`?)
  - File location (only `docs/` directory files changed?)
  - Markdown accessibility (headings, links, alt text, broken links)
  - [TODO] markers (all three removed from welcome.md?)
- Posts a comprehensive comment with:
  - Required checks (must pass)
  - Suggestions (optional improvements)
  - Accessibility analysis (detailed issues + fixes)
  - Learning resources (links to docs)
- Applies labels (documentation, accessibility, needs-review)
- Creates commit status check visible in PR checks

**Visibility:** The bot comment appears in your PR. You see it; the facilitators see it; nobody else does unless they have been added as a collaborator on your repo.

### Step 3: Peer Review (Facilitator-Arranged)

The `learning-room-template` ships with a peer-pairing workflow (`.github/workflows/student-grouping.yml`) that was designed for a single shared repo. Under the GitHub Classroom model used in this workshop, **peer review is arranged by the facilitators rather than auto-assigned**, because each student's repo is private.

When Challenge 3 ("Join the Conversation") or Challenge 8 ("Culture") asks for peer review:

1. The facilitators (Jeff and Michael) pair you with another participant.
2. They add each of you as a collaborator on the other's Learning Room repo.
3. Each of you receives a notification: "You have been added as a collaborator."
4. You can now read the other person's PRs, leave comments, request changes, and approve.
5. After the challenge is complete, the collaborator access remains until the workshop ends -- you can keep helping each other as you work through the rest of Day 1.

#### Visibility

- You see PRs in the repos you have been added to (yours plus any peers you have been paired with)
- Notifications show review requests in your GitHub Notifications inbox
- Other participants in the cohort cannot see your repo unless they are paired with you

### Step 4: Reviewer Reads and Comments

#### Your assigned peer reviewer (when one is paired with you)

1. Receives notification: "PR review requested"
2. Navigates to the PR in your Learning Room repo (they have collaborator access)
3. Reads:
   - PR title: "Complete [TODO] sections in welcome.md"
   - PR description: lists which sections were completed
   - Gandalf's feedback: checks that all `[TODO]` markers are removed, heading hierarchy is valid
   - The actual file changes (Files Changed tab): sees the diff showing old `[TODO]` markers replaced with new content
4. Leaves review comments:
   - Inline comment on the "Who Can Contribute?" paragraph: "Great addition - I especially like the point about AT users bringing valuable perspective."
   - Overall comment: "The content reads well and all TODOs are resolved. One suggestion: the 'Finding Something to Work On' section could mention checking if an issue already has an assignee."
5. Submits review: **Approve** (or **Request Changes** if a `[TODO]` marker was missed)

#### Visibility

- You (the PR author) get a notification: "Your PR has a new review"
- The reviewer's comments appear in your PR thread
- Their name shows in the Reviewers sidebar of your PR

### Step 5: Author Responds and Updates

#### You (PR author)

1. Read Gandalf's feedback and any human review
2. Talks to the reviewer if something is unclear
3. Makes changes based on feedback
4. Pushes new commits to the same branch
5. Re-addresses the feedback

#### Visibility

- Gandalf re-validates on each new commit and updates its comment
- Your reviewer sees the updated activity in the PR
- The PR timeline shows iteration happening

### Step 6: Merge and Celebration

#### When the review is approved (or you decide to self-merge)

- You merge the PR (button becomes available)
- PR closes, shows "merged"

#### Progression Bot Posts the Next Challenge

- The Student Progression bot detects the merged PR and the closed challenge issue
- Posts a celebration comment (challenge badge earned)
- Auto-creates the next challenge issue in your repo so you can keep moving
- Updates the progress tracking file

#### Visibility

- You see the merged PR and the new challenge issue
- Your peer reviewer (if you have one) is notified the PR was merged
- Other participants only see this if they have been paired with you

## The Learning Automation System

When you open a PR in the Learning Room, you get **three types of feedback**:

### Type 1: Automated Bot Feedback (30 seconds)

- Technical validation (links, headings, file locations)
- Accessibility checking (detailed)
- Educational messaging (WHY each thing matters)
- Links to learning resources
- Never fails the PR; always educational

### Type 2: Peer Reviewer Feedback (15-60 minutes)

- Human judgment on content
- Creative suggestions
- Encouragement and mentorship
- Understanding of context
- Can approve, request changes, or comment

### Type 3: Progress Tracking (on merge)

- Skill badges (Markdown Master, Accessibility Advocate)
- Level progression (Beginner → Intermediate → Advanced → Expert)
- Milestone celebrations (1st, 5th, 10th PR)
- Motivational comments

**Together:** Instant technical feedback + human mentorship + visible progress

## FAQ: Pull Requests in Your Learning Room

### "Can I see other students' PRs?"

Not inside their Learning Room repos -- those are private to each student. **You can see other participants' work in two ways:**

- During Challenge 3 ("Join the Conversation") and Challenge 8 ("Culture"), the facilitators pair you with classmates and add you as a collaborator on each other's repos so you can review.
- During Day 2 (and the Bonus C challenge), everyone contributes to the public `accessibility-agents` repo, where every PR is visible to everyone.

### "What if I don't agree with my assigned reviewer?"

When the facilitators pair you for peer review, the pairing is a starting point, not a mandate. You can request additional reviewers manually. Click "Reviewers" -> select someone else, or ask the facilitators to pair you differently.

### "Will my PR get lost when everyone is working at once?"

No. Your repo is your own; you only see your own PRs. Gandalf's feedback is on your PR alone, and any peer reviewer is specifically assigned to you.

### "Can I comment on someone else's PR?"

When the facilitators pair you for review, yes -- you will be added as a collaborator and can comment, approve, and request changes on their PR. On the public `accessibility-agents` repo, anyone can comment on any open PR.

### "What if my reviewer doesn't respond?"

Mention them directly in a PR comment: "@name, any thoughts on the changes I pushed?" Or ask a facilitator to follow up.

### "Can I work with a friend?"

The facilitators arrange peer pairings, but if you know someone else in the cohort and you want to review each other's work, ask either Jeff or Michael to add you to each other's repos.

### "How long does review take?"

When pairings happen during a workshop block, typically 15-60 minutes. If a reviewer is slow, the facilitators can step in or assign someone else.

### "What if bot feedback is wrong?"

Comment on the PR explaining why. Gandalf is intentionally educational, not punitive -- if you disagree with a check, the facilitators can override it. Gandalf is not perfect, which is exactly why human review still matters.

### "Do I need to complete every challenge?"

No. The Learning Room has challenges for all skill levels. You can pick what interests you, complete at your pace, and continue after the workshop -- your repo stays yours.

## If You Get Stuck

| Problem | What to do |
|---|---|
| Cannot find your `learn/<username>` branch | If you have not created it yet, follow Challenge 4. If you created it but cannot see it, refresh the branch selector or run `git fetch origin` from a local clone. |
| Push rejected to main branch | Main is protected. You need to push to your `learn/<username>` branch: `git checkout learn/<your-username>` then push again. |
| I want to see another student's PR | Ask a facilitator -- when peer review is part of a challenge, they will add you as a collaborator on the other student's repo. |
| Practice file has no TODO markers | Verify you are on the correct branch. Run `git branch` to see your current branch. The main branch may have already been updated. |
| Accidentally committed to main | Do not panic. See the failsafe instructions in [Chapter 13](13-how-git-works.md#10-if-you-get-stuck) or ask a facilitator. |
| Everything else | Post a comment on your challenge issue describing what happened. That always counts as participation. |
| I finished Challenge 4 but I am not sure I did it right | Compare your work against the [Challenge 4 reference solution](solutions/solution-04-branch-out.md). Any branch with any name is a success. |
| I finished Challenge 5 but I am not sure I did it right | Compare your work against the [Challenge 5 reference solution](solutions/solution-05-make-your-mark.md). Any clear edit with a descriptive commit message is a success. |
